title: Shantanu and Ganga
hook: seven sons are given to the river while a king keeps his vow of silence; at the eighth, he speaks
carry: the riverbank isn't the whole story

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pratipa, a father's warning, and Shantanu's promise never to stop or question her. A vow made in love.

A son is born to the king and queen. And the queen carries the baby down to the river, and gives him to the Ganga's waters. As she does it, she says it's for his good. Shantanu watches from the bank, and says nothing. He remembers what he promised: never stop her, never speak harshly to her, or she leaves. Another son is born, and the same thing happens. And another. The text tells it plainly, without looking away.
screen: `A SON IS BORN.` → `GIVEN TO THE RIVER.` → `THE KING SAYS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Seven sons, the text says, one after another, into the river. Every time, Shantanu stays silent, afraid that if he speaks, she'll leave him. Then the eighth son is born. As she carries this one toward the river, Shantanu can't hold it in. Don't kill him, he says. Who are you? Why do you kill your own sons? She stops. I won't kill this one, she says. But my time with you is over, as we agreed. And she tells him who she is: Ganga, the daughter of Jahnu, the text says. The sons were the Vasus, cursed to be born as men, and she has freed them as she promised. Two days ago we heard the Vasus ask for this. Yesterday we watched the vow get made. Today we see what it cost, and the scene can be seen three ways. For Shantanu, these were his children, lost in front of him. For the Vasus, it was the release they asked for. For Ganga, it was a promise kept to the letter. The Mahabharata doesn't smooth this over; it lets the scene stay hard. Some readers take it as curses and karma working themselves out. Some hear in it what an unquestioning vow can cost. Some take from it that what's seen from the riverbank isn't the whole story. The son who lives carries the Vasus' power, and their word that he'll have no children. Ganga takes the child with her, and goes.
screen: `SEVEN SONS, AND SILENCE.` · `AT THE EIGHTH, HE SPEAKS.` · `I AM GANGA, DAUGHTER OF JAHNU.` · `THREE VIEWS OF ONE SCENE.` · then, large: `THE RIVERBANK ISN'T THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: This is a hard story, so go gently. Bring to mind something you once watched happen and didn't understand, something that looked only like loss; you don't have to find a hidden meaning in it, because some things stay hard. Just let it be seen, and breathe beside it.
Vasus. The gods cursed to be born as men, given to the river seven times, and spared the eighth when the king finally spoke.
Your line: the riverbank isn't the whole story. Tomorrow, Ganga tells him why. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindu families carry the ashes of their dead to the Ganga, at places such as Haridwar and Varanasi, trusting the river as Ganga is trusted in this story: as a mother whose waters release.

fork.setup: you're Shantanu. your wife carries your eighth son to the river. you promised never to stop her. what do you do?
options: speak up and ask her to stop.
fork.reveal: he speaks. she spares the child, names herself Ganga, and leaves, as their agreement said she would.

original.note: Sanskrit vasu: the Vasus are a group of gods; here, the sons Ganga freed in her waters.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mother who drowns her children.
what it means: a goddess keeping a promise to gods who begged for release, seen through a father's eyes.
what a scholar hears: Ganga names herself daughter of Jahnu, and the spared eighth son carries the Vasus' power.
recall: the Nishada king, Rama's dear friend

chat.says: Why did Ganga give her babies to the river? That sounds so cruel.
options: They were the Vasus, freed as they'd asked; for Shantanu it was still a real loss.
She was angry at Shantanu and wanted to punish him for loving her so much.
A sage ordered her to do it, and she obeyed him against her own wishes.
chat.meaning: Ganga says the sons were the Vasus, freed as she promised. For Shantanu they were his children lost; the story lets both stay true.

Ganga.meaning: the sacred river, and the goddess of the river

Jahnu.meaning: the one Ganga names as her father

Vasus.meaning: a group of gods, cursed to be born as men

karma.meaning: action, and the results that actions bring

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Ganga's sons given to the river; Shantanu speaks at the eighth; Ganga reveals herself)

notes: All paraphrase. Seven sons drowned and the eighth spared are the text's numbers; confirm in Ganguli.
Ganga's words at each drowning are paraphrased as 'for his good'; confirm.
Ganga calls herself daughter of Jahnu in this passage; confirm.
The three 'some readers' takes are unattributed interpretations, given without ranking; a Keeper may wish to adjust them.
The account of Vasishtha's cow and Devavrata's return is left for the following days, which carry the same title.
